rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to elute all 10 compounds if possible and map the overall elution window. This should reveal whether peaks are compressed early, late, or across the full range, guiding the next narrowing or slope adjustment.

All compounds eluted well within the gradient and the main cluster sits around phi_e ≈ 0.11–0.26, so narrowing the gradient window should improve efficiency and reduce the time penalty while keeping all peaks in-gradient. This tests whether the critical mid-cluster pair benefits from a better-matched phi range without changing temperature yet.

The first run already had full resolution, so the main opportunity is reducing analysis time; a much steeper version of the successful broad gradient will show how far runtime can be compressed before the critical 5–8 cluster loses resolution. Comparing this directly to injection 1 isolates slope sensitivity at constant phi window and temperature.

The 10 min gradient is fast but over-compresses the critical 5–7 cluster, while 20 min fully resolves everything but wastes time; 14 min is a direct interpolation to find the best time/resolution tradeoff at the same selectivity. This should recover enough separation for the worst pair while keeping runtime much shorter than injection 1.

The optimum appears to lie between 14 and 20 min, with 14 min just under-resolving the 6/7 pair and 20 min fully resolving it but incurring time penalty. A 16 min gradient should add enough slope relief to push that pair toward baseline resolution while likely keeping run time short enough for a near-maximal CRF.

The critical pair has shown strong slope sensitivity, but a modest temperature change can alter selectivity enough to separate a near-equal-S pair without lengthening the run. Testing 35 C at the current best 14 min method probes whether the 6/7 pair can be improved while preserving the excellent time score.

Lowering temperature worsened selectivity by shifting the bottleneck from 6/7 to 5/6, so the complementary temperature direction is the most informative next test. At the best time setting, 45 C may improve the critical local selectivity enough to beat the 14 min, 40 C method without adding time penalty.

Temperature changes hurt the key selectivity, so the optimum is likely still at 40 C and near the 14–16 min slope range. A 12 min run checks whether the scoring function may still favor a shorter method despite some loss in the 6/7 separation, helping bracket the true optimum around the current best.

Since 35 C and 45 C both worsened the bottleneck but in different ways, one more temperature point below 35 C can map whether selectivity changes monotonically or whether a local optimum exists at lower temperature. Using the proven 14 min gradient isolates temperature effects while preserving a high-efficiency baseline.

Temperature excursions are clearly unfavorable, so return to 40 C and complete the slope bracket above 16 min. This will test whether 16 min was slightly penalized by time while 18 min may still keep a high resolution term and reveal the exact CRF maximum versus gradient time.

Most peaks elute at low effective organic and the last peak is far from the run limit, so trimming only the high end of the gradient may improve where the crowded mid-cluster sits on the slope without adding time. This probes whether a slightly narrower window can boost the 6/7 separation while preserving the excellent runtime of the 14 min method.

Lowering phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 improved the best CRF, so the next logical refinement is another small reduction in the upper endpoint at the same optimal slope/time and temperature. This should test whether the crowded 5–8 region continues to gain selectivity from a tighter high-organic limit without pushing the last peak excessively late.

The phi1 = 0.90 window gave the best balance so far, suggesting improved selectivity versus 0.95 without the extra time cost seen at 0.85. A 12 min gradient on this better window tests whether we can keep enough of that selectivity while shaving runtime further, potentially improving on the current best CRF.

With phi1 = 0.90 established as the best window, the remaining lever is a slightly shallower slope to lift the 6/7 pair above the 14 min result. Testing 16 min at the same window and temperature checks whether the gain in resolution outweighs any modest time penalty and could surpass the current best.

The best method is likely close, but the critical pair remains only marginally resolved; a final extreme temperature test can reveal whether a stronger selectivity shift exists outside the 30–45 C range. Keeping the best phi window and tG fixed isolates this last unexplored temperature lever before focusing entirely on fine window optimization.

The temperature optimum is clearly not below 40 C, but a higher setting than 45 C remains untested and could still improve the marginal 6/7 separation at the best gradient window. This is the last meaningful temperature probe before spending the remaining injections on fine-tuning around the current best method.

With temperature exhausted, the remaining optimization is the gradient window; raising phi0 slightly may reposition the crowded early-mid cluster on a gentler local portion of the gradient while keeping the favorable phi1 = 0.90 endpoint. This tests whether the best method can be improved by trimming the low-organic end rather than the high end.

Raising phi0 to 0.10 improved the best method, so the next fine adjustment is to combine that better low end with a slightly lower phi1, since trimming phi1 helped when phi0 was 0.05. This tests whether a tighter overall window around the actual elution region can nudge the critical 6/7 pair higher without introducing enough delay to hurt CRF.

We have already reached the maximum CRF, so the best strategy now is to map nearby conditions without repeating the optimum. Increasing phi0 one more step tests how sharply tuned the lower endpoint is around the optimum while keeping the successful phi1, tG, and temperature fixed.

A second adjacent optimum at phi0 = 0.15 suggests the lower endpoint may be broadly tolerant, and pushing it one more step will define the edge before the first peak becomes effectively unretained. This continues local mapping around the maximum without risking truncation or large time penalties.

The maximum persists around phi0 = 0.10–0.15 with phi1 = 0.85, so the next nearby probe is to trim the upper endpoint one more step while staying away from the too-high phi0 edge. This defines whether the optimum plateau extends to a narrower high-end window or whether phi1 = 0.85 is already the lower useful limit.

The score plateau spans phi0 = 0.10–0.15 at phi1 = 0.85, and phi1 = 0.80 still gives full resolution with only a tiny time penalty at phi0 = 0.15. Testing phi0 = 0.10 with phi1 = 0.80 maps the remaining corner of this local optimum region and checks whether the slightly lower start can recover the small time loss.

The optimum region appears centered near phi0 = 0.10–0.15 and phi1 = 0.85, but the upper-right neighbor has not been tested. Running phi0 = 0.15 with phi1 = 0.90 completes the local window map around the two maximum-scoring methods and checks whether the score plateau extends upward in phi1.

With the optimum window identified, one remaining question is whether a slightly longer gradient at that window also lands on the score ceiling or incurs a time penalty. This maps the slope dimension directly around one of the two maximum-scoring methods without repeating a prior run.

For the final shot, test the last unprobed slope around the second maximum-scoring window. This determines whether the phi0 = 0.15, phi1 = 0.85 optimum is uniquely tied to 14 min or whether a shorter run can retain enough resolution to stay at the CRF ceiling.
